title: How Do You Plan a Year of Preaching and Sermon Series?
subtitle: On series, seasons, and the long diet you are feeding a congregation, and why planning is not the enemy of the Spirit

sections.title: The Diet You Are Feeding
sections.body:
Think of your preaching not as fifty separate meals but as a diet, the food a congregation lives on year after year, the thing that slowly makes them into one kind of people or another.

No single sermon forms a church. The accumulation does. Over years.

This changes how you think about the pulpit. The question is not only is this Sunday good. The question is what is the whole table doing to these people over a decade. A preacher who only ever picks his favorite texts will feed his people a narrow and lopsided diet, strong in a few places and starved everywhere else, and they will grow up malnourished without knowing why. The congregation cannot ask for what they have never been fed. They do not know they are missing the minor prophets, the hard sayings, the doctrines that are inconvenient to your temperament. You are the one entrusted with the whole counsel of God, and feeding them only the parts you like is a quiet betrayal of that trust. I have preached my favorites for too long and watched a congregation grow thin in the very places I avoided.

sections.title: Planning Is Not Faithlessness
sections.body:
Some preachers refuse to plan, and they wear it as a badge. They wait on the Spirit each week, they say, and to plan a year ahead would be to quench him.

This sounds spiritual. It is usually just unprepared.

The Spirit who leads you on Saturday is the same Spirit who can lead you in January when you plan the year, and there is no reason to believe he only speaks under deadline pressure. Planning is not the enemy of the Spirit. Planning is stewardship, the same stewardship a shepherd shows when he thinks about where the flock will graze next season instead of wandering them into whatever field is closest each morning. The pastor who plans can pray over the whole year, can prepare the hard series properly, can see that he has not touched the gospel of John in eight years, can make sure the congregation gets a real diet and not just whatever his mood served up that week. And planning leaves room for interruption. When the crisis comes, when the moment in the life of the church demands a different word, you set the plan aside and preach the moment, and then you return to the plan. A trellis is not a cage. It is the structure the living thing grows on, and the Spirit is no more quenched by a preaching plan than by a man who decided on Monday to study rather than wait for Saturday's panic.

sections.title: Series, Books, and Balance
sections.body:
Build the year with intention, and the backbone of a healthy diet is consecutive preaching through books of the Bible.

Preach books, not just topics. The text sets the agenda, and that is exactly the point.

When you work through a book in order, the Scripture decides what you preach next, not your preferences and not the pressures of the moment. You are forced into the passages you would have skipped, the ones that challenge you and your people both, and that constraint is a gift. A series gives a congregation something to follow, a sense of going somewhere together, and it lets you build a sustained argument across weeks that a single sermon cannot hold. But balance the diet across the year. Old Testament and New. Narrative and letter. The comforting and the confronting. A long series and then a shorter one, a stretch in the Gospels and then a stretch in the prophets, so the people taste the whole counsel and not one flavor. Watch the length. A series that runs eighteen months will lose them, however good, because no one can hold a single thread that long. Vary the rhythm. Long enough to go deep, short enough to keep them with you.

sections.title: Preaching the Seasons
sections.body:
The year itself preaches, if you let it. There is a rhythm older than your church, the slow turning of the seasons in which the people of God have always retold the one story.

Do not ignore the calendar. Use it. The seasons are a gift the church has handed down for centuries.

Advent teaches a congregation to wait, to sit in the dark and long for a light not yet come, and a people who never learn to wait will not know what to do when God is silent. Lent teaches them to look honestly at their own sin and their own mortality, the season the modern church most wants to skip and most needs. Easter is the center, the empty tomb that the whole faith stands or falls on, and it deserves your best every single year. These seasons are not empty ritual unless you preach them emptily. They are a way of walking the congregation through the gospel story annually, of letting the shape of the year disciple them in the shape of the faith. You do not have to follow the calendar slavishly. But to ignore it entirely is to throw away a tested tool that teaches your people the rhythm of dying and rising they are meant to live.

sections.title: The People You Are Forming
sections.body:
Step back and remember what the plan is for, because it is easy to fall in love with the system and forget the souls. You are not assembling a curriculum. You are forming a people.

In ten years, the people in front of you will largely be what your preaching has made them. That is a sobering thing to hold.

So plan with their formation in mind, not just your interests. What do these people need to become over the next decade, and what diet will get them there. They need to know the whole story, not fragments. They need the hard texts that will hold them when life turns hard. They need to be fed the gospel so relentlessly that it sinks past their heads into the places where they actually live. This is a long obedience, the unglamorous faithfulness of feeding the same people week after week, year after year, when no single Sunday seems to change anything. Most of it you will never see bear fruit, because formation is slow and quiet and the harvest often comes after you are gone. Plan anyway. Feed them faithfully anyway. You are setting a table that will form a people long after you have stopped setting it, and the God who gives the growth is keeping a record you cannot see.
